sections.h2: Where is the Holmes County Recorder, and what does the office keep?
sections.html:
The Holmes County Recorder works at 75 E. Clinton Street, Suite 101, in Millersburg, OH 44654. The phone is (330) 674-5916 and the fax is (330) 674-0782. The office takes cash, check and credit card, and the county site says that covers deeds and other conveyance papers.

Millersburg is the county seat, and Holmes was carved out of Coshocton, Tuscarawas and Wayne counties in 1824. The county page lists what the Recorder holds:

  • deeds, mortgages and leases
  • mechanic's, workers' compensation, unemployment and federal tax liens
  • partnerships, soldier's discharges and UCC financing statements
  • plats

A seller rarely visits all of these. For a house sale, the deed and any mortgage release are the papers that matter, and both end up in Suite 101.

sections.h2: Why does a deed in Holmes County go through so many offices?
sections.html:
Holmes County requires every real estate description to be reviewed before the Auditor and Recorder see it. The county's conveyance standards, effective March 1, 2019, say Tax Map Office approval comes first for all descriptions, plats, land contracts, mineral deeds and easements for ingress and egress.

That review matters in a county where farms are often split and resold. Wikipedia reports that Holmes holds the highest concentration of Amish in the world, about 48% of residents in 2020, and the Census Bureau counts 3.26 persons per household here, the largest of the four Ohio counties compared on its QuickFacts page. A hand-me-down farm parcel with an old metes and bounds description is the kind of paper the Tax Map Office checks line by line.

Plan on a full workday for each submission. The standards allow 24 hours from drop-off to pick-up and warn that long or complex documents can take more. A preliminary review of a draft is encouraged so the final deed does not bounce.

sections.h2: In what order do the Holmes County offices handle a deed?
sections.html:
The county's conveyance-by-mail sheet sets four steps, and each step is a separate office with its own forms and fees. Paper that arrives by mail needs a pre-addressed, stamped envelope for every office along the way.

StepOfficeWhereWhat it does
1Tax Map Office75 E. Clinton St., Suite 102, (330) 674-6631Reviews the description, 24-hour period
2Planning Commission2 Court St., Suite 2, (330) 674-8625Stamps documents that need its approval
3County Auditor75 E. Clinton St., Suite 107Collects conveyance and transfer fees
4County Recorder75 E. Clinton St., Suite 101Records the deed

Source: Holmes County conveyance-by-mail instructions. The Auditor checks for the Tax Map and Planning Commission stamps before processing, so a skipped step stops the whole file.

sections.h2: What does the Holmes County Auditor charge when a house sells?
sections.html:
The schedule in the county's standards lists a conveyance fee of $4.00 per thousand dollars of the sale price and a transfer fee of $0.50 per parcel described on the document. The schedule is labeled as of January 1, 1989, so ask the Auditor to confirm both figures before closing.

Ohio law puts the cost on the seller. R.C. 319.202(D) says the grantor pays the auditor's conveyance fee and any county transfer tax levied under Chapter 322.

  • Pay the Auditor by check made out to the Holmes County Auditor, and keep recording fees on a separate check.
  • The office cannot make change on an overwritten check and will not take a blank check to fill in later.
  • A stopped check on a transfer is referred to the county Prosecutor.
  • Bring the DTE 100 statement, or the DTE 100EX if the transfer is exempt, plus DTE 101 for homestead property and DTE 102 for current agricultural use land.

A manufactured or mobile home has an extra hurdle: the Auditor will not transfer one without the County Treasurer's stamp showing its taxes are paid.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to record a deed in Holmes County?
sections.html:
The Recorder's announcements page shows the last fee notice it posted: since October 17, 2019, most documents cost $34.00 for the first two pages plus $8.00 for each added page, under R.C. 317.32 and 317.36. The statute was amended again by Senate Bill 94, effective October 24, 2024, and it now lets a county add a document preservation surcharge of up to five dollars. Ask the Recorder for the total for your page count.

The format rules in R.C. 317.114 can add cost. A paper that fails them is still accepted, but the Recorder collects an extra $10.00 for its services and another $10.00 for the Ohio Housing Trust Fund. The rules are:

  • type no smaller than size ten, black or blue ink, no highlighting
  • paper from 8.5 by 11 inches up to 8.5 by 14 inches
  • one-inch margins on both sides and the bottom
  • a three-inch blank margin at the top of the first page and 1.5 inches on later pages

Court and taxing-authority documents, plats, DD-214 discharges and state or federal documents are outside the rule.

sections.h2: How can I search Holmes County records or record a deed electronically?
sections.html:
The Recorder offers two online search tools, AVA and Laredo Anywhere. AVA needs no login and suits an occasional search. Laredo Anywhere is built for frequent users, and the county keeps a setup guide in its document library.

Images of deeds, easements, rights-of-way and leases can be viewed and printed in both tools. Other document types are viewable from 1980 to the present. Plats are on the Tax Map Department site rather than in the Recorder's search.

The office accepts electronic documents, deeds included. The county names four vendors: ePN, Simplifile, Indecomm Global Services and CSC. These services are meant for title companies, law firms and banks that record regularly. R.C. 317.13 required every Ohio recorder to offer electronic recording of conveyance papers by June 30, 2026, and that date has passed.

sections.h2: What do the Holmes County numbers say about owning and selling here?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau estimates Holmes County at 44,970 people for July 1, 2025, up 1.7% from the April 2020 base. QuickFacts lists 14,592 housing units, an owner-occupied rate of 79.0%, and a median owner-occupied value of $267,700 for 2020 to 2024. Median household income is $76,140.

Two other figures shape how a sale gets paperwork done. Only 63.5% of households have a broadband subscription, the lowest among the four counties on that comparison, and 49.0% of residents age five and older speak a language other than English at home. Paper filing and phone calls to the offices in Suite 101, 102 and 107 remain the practical route for many families.

Tourism supports the local economy, and Wikipedia notes Holmes ranked as Ohio's second most popular tourist destination in 2017. Berlin, home to the Amish and Mennonite Heritage Center, is one of the draws.

faqs.q: Does the Holmes County Recorder accept credit cards for a deed?
faqs.a: Yes. The Recorder's overview page says the office accepts cash, check and credit card, and that this includes deeds and other conveyance documents.

faqs.q: Do I need Tax Map Office approval before I record a deed in Holmes County?
faqs.a: Yes, for any document that carries a legal description of real estate. The county's conveyance standards send all descriptions, land contracts, mineral deeds and easements to the Tax Map Office first, with a 24-hour review period.

faqs.q: Who pays the conveyance fee on a Holmes County sale?
faqs.a: The seller. R.C. 319.202(D) makes the grantor responsible for the auditor's conveyance fee, and the Auditor's schedule lists $4.00 per thousand dollars of the sale price plus $0.50 per parcel, dated January 1, 1989. Confirm the current figures with the Auditor.

faqs.q: Can I deliver a Holmes County deed by mail?
faqs.a: Yes. The county's conveyance-by-mail sheet lists the four offices in order, and each one needs its own forms, fees and a pre-addressed envelope with correct postage.

faqs.q: Can anyone get a copy of a military discharge recorded in Holmes County?
faqs.a: No. Under R.C. 317.24, a recorded discharge is not a public record for 75 years. Only authorized parties, such as the veteran, a county veterans service officer or an heir of a deceased veteran, can get an unredacted copy, and others see only name, rank, date of birth, date of discharge and type of discharge.
